opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the most compelling part is that you can actually watch it think. When you hand Operator a task, say booking a restaurant or filling out some tedious form, you're not just getting a final answer back. You see it move the cursor, read the page, decide where to click, hit a dead end, back up, and try something else. It's a little like watching a new employee on their first day. Sometimes you're impressed, and sometimes you want to lean over and say, "No, no, the button's right there."

What gets me is that this is a different interaction model from what we've had with language models so far. With a chat interface, the model gives you text and you're the one who goes and does something with it. With Operator, the model is the one taking actions in the world, or at least in the browser, which for a lot of knowledge work is basically the world. That shift from "tell me what to do" to "go do it" is a big deal, even if the current version is still pretty rough around the edges.

I also find the failures really instructive. When it gets stuck, it's usually not because it doesn't understand the goal. It's because the web is messy. There are pop-ups, weird layouts, CAPTCHAs, and forms that behave unexpectedly. Watching that tells you a lot about where the real bottlenecks are for agents. It's less about raw intelligence and more about robustness, recovery from errors, and knowing when to stop and ask the human for help. Those are exactly the problems we'll have to solve to make agents genuinely useful. So for me it's a window into both how far we've come and how much work is still left.

r001.rationale: The response says you can “watch it think” as Operator reads pages, decides where to click, and recovers from dead ends, making its intelligence perceptible through humanlike website interaction.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that's compelling about it is that it's one of the first times you really get to watch an AI agent think out loud in a domain that everyone understands. Like, when you watch a coding agent, unless you're a programmer, it's kind of abstract what it's doing. But everybody knows what a browser is. Everybody knows what it looks like to go to a website, click on a button, fill in a form, hit submit. So when you watch Operator do that, you can see very concretely where it's doing well and where it's struggling in a way that's really legible.

And I think the second thing is, it exposes how much of the task is actually in the long tail of weird little decisions. Like, if you ask it to book you a restaurant reservation, the hard part isn't typing the restaurant name into the search box. The hard part is, you know, there's a popup that shows up, or the date picker is weird, or there are three restaurants with the same name and it has to figure out which one you meant. And watching the model navigate those moments, sometimes gracefully and sometimes not, gives you a really visceral sense of where the capability frontier actually is right now. It's one thing to read a benchmark number. It's another thing to watch the model stare at a cookie consent banner for thirty seconds trying to figure out what to do.

And then honestly, the last piece is just that it's a preview of the interaction model. For most of the history of this technology, the loop has been you type, model responds, you type again. With Operator, you give it a goal, and then you're sort of a supervisor. You're watching, you're deciding when to intervene, you're deciding how much to trust it. And I think that shift, from being the one doing the work to being the one overseeing the work, is going to be a big part of how people relate to these systems going forward. So watching it is partly compelling because of what the model does, and partly compelling because of what it tells you about what your own role is about to become.

r001.rationale: The response says watching Operator navigate familiar website actions makes its performance and struggles concrete and legible to viewers, communicating how its website interaction makes its intelligence perceptible.

astra-6.text:
What’s compelling to me is that you can actually watch it work through a problem. It clicks around, looks at what happened, and decides what to do next. And sometimes it gets something wrong and has to backtrack. There’s something really striking about seeing that loop play out in a browser, in the same interface you would use yourself.

It also makes the limitations very tangible. You can see a task that’s easy for a person take a lot of steps, or watch it get stuck somewhere you wouldn’t expect. So you get both this sense of how powerful the technology could be and a pretty concrete picture of what still needs to improve.

r001.rationale: It describes Operator clicking through a browser, observing results, choosing what to do next, and sometimes backtracking in the same interface a person would use—making its problem-solving visible to someone watching.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s compelling to me is watching it close the loop. It takes an action, looks at what happened, and then decides what to do next. And when something unexpected happens—a page looks different, or a button isn’t where it expected—you get to see whether it can recover.

That’s a different experience from asking a model a question and getting an answer. You’re watching it try to accomplish something over time. And you can see both the promise and the limitations pretty clearly: a step can look really impressive, but completing the whole task reliably requires getting a lot of those steps right.

r001.rationale: The response describes Operator taking actions on pages, observing results, and recovering from surprises, but does not identify humanlike website interaction as what makes its intelligence perceptible.
